Retail traders “have not been a ballast. We’ve talked a lot about how they do this ‘buy the dip’; they’re the support” for the broader market, Amy Wu Silverman, head of derivatives strategy at RBC Capital Markets, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box.” “Not only was that absent, it was going the other way.”

“When you look at Thursday’s price action, it was kicked off by a lot of retail put buying. It was retail who got nervous and this sort of created a chain reaction with other aspects of the market,” Silverman said.

@C_Barraud's Wednesday Brief also included the WSJ’s Nick Timiraos noting that in contrast with what we've heard from other Fed officials of late, Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman struck “a cautious note.” His post has a link to her speech, though, which makes it clear she's likely on board with another hike, but she does provide more caveats and a dose of caution about the AI trade.

▪️ Importantly, she stresses there is more work to do: “Today, I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming. This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2 percent.” She says Tuesday's CPI suggests core PCE “likely moved up further to 3.3 percent in October,” that pressures “may be broadening,” and that she’s “more attentive to the inflation side of our mandate.”

▪️ Her caveats: Financial conditions “have tightened a bit recently,” so “the benefit of additional policy tightening has to be carefully weighed against its costs for interest-rate-sensitive sectors.” Bowman also sees tariffs, energy and AI each driving “roughly one-fourth” of above-target core PCE and says "my approach is to look through temporary energy-driven inflation, when possible, and to remain alert to signs that it is spreading into broader prices or expectations." Currently she mostly views those pressures as“relative price shocks in specific sectors,” and she expects core PCE “to move closer to 2 percent next year.”

▪️ The AI trade: Risks “seem to be concentrated in only a few large firms that provide AI services.” AI-related debt “is on track to exceed $800 billion this year,” and other obligations are “more than three times” that. Equity stakes in customers are “creating the appearance of circular financing.” A shortfall in AI revenues could bring “a sharp correction in equity prices for AI firms, higher financing costs, and reduced access to credit.”

So she seems in the hike camp, just not the faster-hike camp.

@C_Barraud’s Wednesday Brief flagged JPMorgan’s latest Global Equity Strategy note (via ZeroHedge), where Dubravko Lakos-Bujas, who warned in May that momentum crowding had hit a 40-year high, now says “the capitulation process is far along.” He’s dropped his caution on momentum and kept his 8,000 S&P 500 target, about 6% above Tuesday’s close.

The damage:
▪️ JPMorgan’s momentum winners lagged the market by 10.8% in October, the worst month in data back to 1985.
▪️ Both sides lost at once: the longs fell 12% while the shorts rallied 5%, so long/short momentum fell 16% on the month. It’s now down 38.4% from its June peak, the deepest drawdown since ChatGPT launched.
▪️ October 22 alone was a 6.6 standard deviation down day.

JPMorgan’s capitulation checklist:
▪️ Momentum crowding fell from the 100th to the 76th percentile against 40 years of history, the largest unwind since the post-GFC recovery. Against the past year, it’s at the 0th.
▪️ Leveraged ETFs sold about $60B Thursday, the second most on record, after more than $35B the Friday before. Their exposure is now below where it started the year.
▪️ CTAs are already short US stocks, and vol-targeting funds cut leverage from the 65th percentile to the 30th.
▪️ The QQQ’s RSI dropped below 30 Thursday. In the nine prior cases over the past three years, the QQQ gained about 4% on average over the next five sessions. Monday’s 2.4% S&P 500 gain was a start.
▪️ Not cleared yet: JPMorgan estimates vol-control funds still have about $50B to sell, and dealer gamma sits in the 12th percentile, leaving risks “two-way.”

The reset also hit valuations. The S&P 500’s forward P/E fell from 21.2 in May to 17.9 with earnings estimates roughly flat, while the 61 upstream AI stocks ($12.5T) went from 24.3x to 12.0x, with memory at just 3.2x. 

JPMorgan’s trade is long 12-month momentum against short 3-month momentum, meaning buy the crushed AI hardware and sell the pharma and energy names investors hid in. The catch: if semis just go sideways, quant rebalancing turns into a source of selling by 2Q27.

Christophe Barraud (@C_Barraud) sums up the NY Fed’s third-quarter household debt report saying US household credit stress “remains elevated, but the picture varies significantly across loan categories.” The data back this up, showing a shift in where new delinquencies are coming from: less in credit cards, more in mortgages and autos.

The headline: household debt jumped $334 billion (1.8%) to a record $19.105 trillion, the biggest increase since the fourth quarter of 2022, after a $13 billion dip in the second quarter.

Of that, 4.96% is in some stage of delinquency, the highest since the first quarter of 2016, up from 4.73% (the NY Fed rounds it to 5.0%, a 0.3-point rise).

▪️ Credit cards: Balances rose $22 billion to a record $1.285 trillion (up 4.22% year-over-year), but limits rose $115 billion, so utilization fell to 22.65%, the lowest since the second quarter of 2023. As Barraud notes, 12.90% of card balances are 90 or more days late, close to the 13.74% peak in the second quarter of 2010. But the rate of card balances newly turning seriously delinquent fell to 6.87%, the lowest since the first quarter of 2024. That shows the stabilization in new card defaults he flags.

▪️ Autos: 5.66% of auto balances are 90 or more days late, a record for data going back to 2003. The rate turning seriously delinquent rose to 3.02%, the highest since the first quarter of 2010.

▪️ Mortgages: 
-Balances rose $257 billion to a record $13.374 trillion, the most since the third quarter of 2022, on $595 billion of new mortgages, also the most since the third quarter of 2022. With many homeowners locked into low-rate mortgages, home equity lines of credit rose $23 billion to $481 billion, the largest increase since 2005. 
-Mortgage delinquencies are low at 1.13%, as Barraud says, but that’s up from 0.99% and the highest since the first quarter of 2018. The rate of mortgage balances turning seriously delinquent rose to 1.60%, the highest since the third quarter of 2015, and foreclosures rose to 61,900, the most since the first quarter of 2020.

▪️ Student loans: 10.92% are 90 or more days late, distorted by the restart of credit reporting, as he notes. The rate turning seriously delinquent eased to 7.72%, the lowest since delinquencies began reappearing in early 2025.

TransUnion’s third-quarter credit report backs up the housing trend and adds a catch on cards. The share of mortgage borrowers 60 or more days late rose to 1.64% from 1.36% a year earlier. On cards, the share of balances 90 or more days late fell to 1.99% from 2.05%, but the share of borrowers that far behind rose to 2.50% from 2.37%. More people are falling behind, just on smaller balances, so the dollar-based improvement flatters the picture.

So as of the third quarter, card stress remained high but was no longer building, while housing and autos were where it was growing. The rate of new serious mortgage delinquencies is still far below its 2009 peak of 8.35%, but it has climbed in all but one quarter since late 2021, and fewer late borrowers are catching up (37.31% of mortgages 30 to 60 days late got current, down from 42.04%).

That fits with the NY Fed’s October consumer survey, where households’ expected odds of missing a debt payment jumped to 13.8%, the highest since December 2025.

“Spot down, vol down” at that size is rare: just 4% of comparable S&P 500 down days since 1990, and the first since March 2025.

Note: The VVIX also fell, but adding that to the analysis doesn't change things.

Caveat: Small sample size.

@C_Barraud's Tuesday Brief flagged an FT story on SoftBank’s surprise $7B quarterly loss, which shows that data center costs were rising well before the midterm elections

SoftBank’s $7B loss (vs. a ~$535M profit expected) included a $3.7B writedown of non-refundable advance payments for gas turbines, grid equipment and turbine manufacturing slots, tied in part to its Ports-Pike data center campus in Pike County, Ohio. SoftBank blamed the “evolving requirements” of its projects. The Brief notes its CFO said there’s been no talk of downsizing Ohio and that up to $2.1B could come back as rebates.

▪ PJM, the grid covering Ohio and 12 other states plus DC, saw its capacity price go from $28.92/MW-day for 2024/25 to $269.92 for 2025/26, about 9x.
▪ The next three auctions all cleared at the cap, at $329.17, $333.44 and $325, which locks high prices in through May 2029.
▪ Without the cap, PJM estimates the 2028/29 price would have been $554.72, 71% higher.
▪ PJM’s market monitor attributes $21.3B, or 45%, of the $47.2B in capacity costs from the last three auctions to data center load forecasts.
▪ That has helped electricity CPI outrun core CPI in every published month since June 2025. 
▪ Today’s October CPI showed electricity up another 0.9% m/m vs. 0.3% for core.

The FT says the backlash over data centers pushing up power bills helped Democrats retake Congress. But the squeeze didn’t start with the election. It’s been in the data since mid-2025 and is locked into PJM prices through mid-2029. Ohio took action as long ago as July 2025 when regulators approved AEP Ohio’s tariff, making large new data centers pay for most of the power they contract for, whether or not they use it. This will likely be seen in Texas and other data center hot spots.

And power is just one of many costs that will likely flow through to earnings results in coming quarters.

Despite nominal cash earnings seeing the largest increase since 1997 in September, Japan’s household spending unexpectedly fell by the most since 2020, and expected rate hikes from the BoJ will only add to pressure on households.

Outlays by households adjusted for inflation declined 6.8% in September from a year earlier, led by transport, education and entertainment. It was the 10th straight month of falling year-over-year spending.

“Households are still vulnerable to concerns about rising prices,” said Takeshi Minami, chief economist at the Norinchukin Research Institute. “Since wages are rising, it’s hard to explain why consumer spending isn’t picking up.”

“It’s a difficult call whether the BOJ should accelerate the pace of interest rate hikes just focusing on strong AI-related demand, while consumer spending remains weak,” said Minami.
